# Command line (/docs/cli)

`tgd` is the command line of teigeodata: one static binary that looks inside packs, checks them,
cuts smaller ones, answers every query in text, JSON, GeoJSON or Nominatim's format, installs and
updates packs in the store, and serves them over [HTTP](/docs/servers/http) and
[MCP](/docs/servers/mcp).

<Callout title="Every example on this page ran">
The commands below are cut from one script, [tour.sh](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/blob/main/site/examples/cli/tour.sh),
which CI runs on the released pack `world-np-lite.tgd` and checks against the output shown.
</Callout>

## Install [#install]

```sh
cargo install --locked teigeodata-cli
```

It installs from crates.io; there are no prebuilt `tgd` binaries yet. `tgd completions zsh` (or `bash`,
`fish`, `powershell`, `elvish`) prints a completion script.

Every query takes `--pack <file>` (repeat it for several packs). Where packs disagree, the
[layer rule](/docs/concepts/packs#layers) decides, not their order: the newer release, then the
more specific pack. Without one, it answers from the packs installed in the [store](#the-store).

## Look inside a pack [#look-inside-a-pack]

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd inspect "$PACK" | sed -n '1,4p'
```

```text title="Output"
world baseline 2026.11.14  (15641408 bytes, format 0.1, created 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z)
unsigned
licence: "cc-by-4.0"
attribution: 11 notices
```

The full listing goes on with every source's notice, every section with its component and size,
and the bytes of each component. `tgd verify <pack>` checks the head and every section's hash
(`--deep` also decodes every value, `--key` checks the signature); `tgd diff <old> <new>` lists
what changed between two releases, section by section and place by place.

## Search [#search]

A name, in any script or spelling. `-k` is how many:

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd search Pokhara -k 3 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Pokhara  settlement  28.266890,83.968000  tgd:np/1xhb  1006 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 132
Pokhara  admin 3  28.209407,83.981817  tgd:np/1xnr  842 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 105
Pokhara  settlement  28.063631,82.378569  tgd:np/15t1  612 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 90
```

Each line is the name, the kind (and admin level), the point, the ID, the elevation with how it
was found (`model` from the terrain, `surveyed` from a source), the timezone and the score.
Write a parent after a comma to rank the places inside it first:

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd search "Kathmandu, Bagmati" -k 2 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Kathmandu  settlement  27.701690,85.320600  tgd:np/2cn  1288 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 1144
Kathmandu  admin 3  27.708951,85.324957  tgd:np/2gm  1308 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 1136
```

`--focus lat,lon` ranks places near a point first: at the focus a place gains 30 points, and the
gain halves every `--scale-km` (50 by default). `--strict` ranks by how well the name matched
before anything else.

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd search Shivapur -k 3 --focus 28.7,80.6 --scale-km 30 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Shivapur  settlement  28.531014,80.821273  tgd:np/2v99  153 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 105
Shivapur  settlement  28.714055,80.986874  tgd:np/2raj  193 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 103
Shivapur  settlement  28.506089,81.303187  tgd:np/2rkx  179 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 96
```

## A place by its ID [#a-place-by-its-id]

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd get tgd:np/1xhb --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Pokhara  settlement  28.266890,83.968000  tgd:np/1xhb  1006 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
```

Every query prints JSON with `--json`: one record per place, nulls where a value is unknown.

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd get tgd:np/1xhb --json --pack "$PACK"
```

```json title="Output"
[
{"id":"tgd:np/1xhb","name":"Pokhara","kind":"settlement","admin_level":0,"lat":28.26689,"lon":83.968,"elevation":1006,"elevation_source":"model","parent":"tgd:np/1xnr","timezone":"Asia/Kathmandu"}
]
```

## From a point [#from-a-point]

`reverse` gives the nearest places with their distance and bearing (from the place to the point,
"3.2 km at 45° from Pokhara"); `inside` marks a place that holds the point: a unit by its
outline, a settlement or locality within its radius of the point. `--in-country` never crosses a border.

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd reverse 27.7172 85.3240 -k 3 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Narayanhiti Royal Palace  settlement  27.718504,85.320980  tgd:np/2h3  1309 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  330.8 m away at 116°  inside
Gairidhara  settlement  27.719775,85.326454  tgd:np/2h2  1306 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  374.6 m away at 220.2°
Naxal  settlement  27.714251,85.326034  tgd:np/2gh  1308 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  384.2 m away at 328.6°
```

`near` does the same from a place:

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd near tgd:np/2cn -k 3 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Bhrikuti Mandap  settlement  27.703020,85.319798  tgd:np/2ga  1298 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  167.6 m away at 151.9°
Bagbazar  settlement  27.704485,85.318880  tgd:np/2g9  1298 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  353.9 m away at 151.4°
Shahidgate  settlement  27.699626,85.317360  tgd:np/2cp  1295 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  393 m away at 54.3°
```

`admin` gives every unit that holds the point, country first:

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd admin 28.2096 83.9856 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Nepal  country NP  28.000000,84.000000  tgd:np/1wmc  1046 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
Gandaki  admin 1 NP-P4  28.384514,84.035774  tgd:np/2922  2689 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
Kaski  admin 2  28.345513,83.970886  tgd:np/295c  1231 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
Pokhara  admin 3  28.209407,83.981817  tgd:np/1xnr  842 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
```

## Timezone and elevation [#timezone-and-elevation]

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd tz 27.7172 85.3240 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Asia/Kathmandu  timezone_area  28.397480,83.093537  tgd:np/1gce  Asia/Kathmandu  UTC+05:45 (+0545)
```

`tgd tz` also takes a place ID. The offset is computed from the tzdb rules inside the pack, at
the current time.

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd elevation 27.7172 85.3240 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
1304.2 m above EGM2008 (NASADEM, 464 m spacing)
```

## GeoJSON and Nominatim [#geojson-and-nominatim]

`--geojson` prints a FeatureCollection (RFC 7946) ready for MapLibre, Leaflet or QGIS, with the
attribution at its top level:

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd search Pokhara -k 1 --geojson --pack "$PACK"
```

```json title="Output"
{"type":"FeatureCollection","attribution":"Made with Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com), public domain\nGeoNames (https://www.geonames.org), CC BY 4.0\nTime zones: IANA Time Zone Database 2026f (public domain)\nWikidata (https://www.wikidata.org), CC0 1.0\nUnicode CLDR (https://cldr.unicode.org), Copyright © 1991-2026 Unicode, Inc., under the Unicode License v3\nLocal Government Directory, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Government of India (https://lgdirectory.gov.in)\nAdministrative boundaries: Survey Department of Nepal and UN Resident Coordinator's Office in Nepal, via OCHA HDX (cod-ab-npl), CC BY-IGO 3.0\nElevation: NASADEM, NASA JPL and LP DAAC\nBuildings: Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (https://cdla.dev/permissive-2-0/)\nBuildings: Google Open Buildings v3 (Sirko et al. 2021, arXiv:2107.12283), CC BY 4.0\nCentral Bureau of Statistics (now National Statistics Office), Nepal, via Open Data Nepal (https://opendatanepal.com), Creative Commons Attribution","features":[
{"type":"Feature","id":"tgd:np/1xhb","geometry":{"type":"Point","coordinates":[83.968,28.26689]},"properties":{"id":"tgd:np/1xhb","name":"Pokhara","kind":"settlement","admin_level":0,"elevation":1006,"elevation_source":"model","parent":"tgd:np/1xnr","timezone":"Asia/Kathmandu","score":132}}
]}
```

`--nominatim` prints Nominatim's `json` format, so tools written for Nominatim read the output
unchanged:

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd reverse 28.2096 83.9856 -k 1 --nominatim --pack "$PACK"
```

```json title="Output"
[
  {
    "address": {
      "admin_level_1": "Gandaki",
      "admin_level_2": "Kaski",
      "admin_level_3": "Pokhara",
      "country": "Nepal",
      "country_code": "np"
    },
    "boundingbox": [
      "28.210016",
      "28.210016",
      "83.987089",
      "83.987089"
    ],
    "display_name": "Prithvi-chowk, Pokhara, Kaski, Gandaki, Nepal",
    "lat": "28.210016",
    "licence": "Made with Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com), public domain; GeoNames (https://www.geonames.org), CC BY 4.0; Time zones: IANA Time Zone Database 2026f (public domain); Wikidata (https://www.wikidata.org), CC0 1.0; Unicode CLDR (https://cldr.unicode.org), Copyright © 1991-2026 Unicode, Inc., under the Unicode License v3; Local Government Directory, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Government of India (https://lgdirectory.gov.in); Administrative boundaries: Survey Department of Nepal and UN Resident Coordinator's Office in Nepal, via OCHA HDX (cod-ab-npl), CC BY-IGO 3.0; Elevation: NASADEM, NASA JPL and LP DAAC; Buildings: Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (https://cdla.dev/permissive-2-0/); Buildings: Google Open Buildings v3 (Sirko et al. 2021, arXiv:2107.12283), CC BY 4.0; Central Bureau of Statistics (now National Statistics Office), Nepal, via Open Data Nepal (https://opendatanepal.com), Creative Commons Attribution",
    "lon": "83.987089",
    "name": "Prithvi-chowk",
    "place_id": "tgd:np/1xnp"
  }
]
```

## Cut a smaller pack [#cut-a-smaller-pack]

`extract` writes a pack of the places in a box (with their ancestors and timezone areas), of some
components, or both. The new pack is a normal pack: every query works on it.

```sh title="tour.sh"
tgd extract "$PACK" --bbox 85.2,27.6,85.5,27.8 --out kathmandu.tgd
tgd search Kathmandu -k 1 --pack kathmandu.tgd
```

```text title="Output"
wrote kathmandu.tgd: 428900 bytes, 14 sections, 1388 places; components point,elevation,admin,names,search,timezone,timezone-index,boundaries,admin-index,postal,dem,extra,tz-rules,substring,dem-coarse
Kathmandu  settlement  27.701690,85.320600  tgd:np/2cn  1288 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 144
```

`--components point,names` keeps only those components and what they need; with `--bbox`,
`--lod 3` stores coarser boundaries. `tgd export <pack>` streams every place out, in the order the pack stores
them.

## Postal codes [#postal-codes]

`tgd postal 44600` finds the places a code names; `--prefix` completes a partial code;
`tgd postal <lat> <lon>` gives the codes at a point. Codes are matched with or without
separators, in any case and in any script's digits.

## The store [#the-store]

The store keeps installed packs and the signed catalog that says which exist. It lives in the
platform's data directory, or where `--store` or `TEIGEODATA_STORE` says.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `tgd init` | Set up the store: the catalog's mirrors and its trusted root. |
| `tgd refresh [--countries a,b]` | Fetch what changed in the catalog. |
| `tgd catalog` | List the catalog's packs, offline. |
| `tgd find <name>` | Find a place by name with the packs that hold it, offline: what to install for "Dubai". |
| `tgd locate <lat> <lon>` | The countries at a point, with their packs. |
| `tgd install <packs>` | Install packs and their dependencies; `--components`, `--names` and `--outlines` install a part. |
| `tgd update` | Update installed packs to the catalog's releases. |
| `tgd remove`, `tgd pin` | Remove a pack (and what nothing else needs), or keep one when room is made. |
| `tgd status`, `tgd repair` | The installed packs and their health; fetch what a damaged one lacks. |

The signed catalog goes live with the first catalog release; until then, packs are downloaded
from the data releases and opened with `--pack`. See [the store](/docs/concepts/store).

## Serve [#serve]

`tgd serve` answers every query over HTTP, and `tgd mcp` over MCP for AI agents: see
[HTTP server](/docs/servers/http) and [MCP server](/docs/servers/mcp).

# Accuracy (/docs/concepts/accuracy)

teigeodata's data is built to be right first, then complete. Each kind of answer has a target,
and each target is a **gate**: a build that misses it fails, and the measured figures ship in
each pack's summary.

## The order of importance [#the-order-of-importance]

1. **Coordinates and elevation.** A place's height is read from the terrain at its point, so the
   two are judged together: the target is a vertical error of at most 50 m at the 90th
   percentile. Because the height error is mostly the position error times the slope, the point
   targets follow from it: a populated place within 500 m of its settlement core (P90) on gentle
   ground and within 150 m where the slope is 5° or steeper; an admin unit's point always inside
   its own outline.
2. **Names.** Spellings follow each country's official sources and its lexicon, each rule with its
   source. Search is measured on a curated set of real queries per country (golden queries) for
   how often the right place comes first.
3. **Population**, where it is published. Optional values are null rather than guessed.

## How heights are found [#how-heights-are-found]

Every place's `elevation` is sampled from a digital elevation model at the place's point,
bilinearly, in metres above EGM2008 (mean sea level). The source tells you how it was found:
`model` from the terrain, `surveyed` from a source that measured it (summits keep their surveyed
height where it agrees with the terrain). The lite build uses NASADEM; the main build Copernicus
GLO-30.

`elevation_at` reads the finest grid a pack has at the point: a country's 1″ grid (about 30 m)
where its terrain pack is installed, and the world's coarse 15″ grid (about 460 m) everywhere
else. Measured on Nepal (2026-11-12), the coarse grid is within 61 m of the fine one at P90 and
110 m at P99: enough for sunrise and sunset times, not for hiking. Install the country's `dem`
component where heights must be precise.

## Timezones [#timezones]

Zones are the IANA tz database's, at the release each pack names (`tz_version`), and offsets are
computed from the tzdb rules in the pack, not from the device. The lite build draws a country with
one zone over that country's outline; the main build uses the zone boundaries of
timezone-boundary-builder. Each build is checked against an independent source.

## Boundaries and perspective [#boundaries-and-perspective]

Boundaries are the official ones where they are open, stored as shared arcs so neighbouring
units never overlap or leave gaps. Where a boundary is disputed, teigeodata draws it from one
stated perspective: Nepal's official map of 2020, including Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura.
The perspective is recorded in each country's profile, with its sources.

## Measured, per country [#measured-per-country]

Every pack's summary states its rows, the sources of every field, the share of places with a
name in each language, and the gates it passed. The [data pages](/docs/data) collect them per
country and release.

A few ideas explain everything teigeodata does. Each page is short.

# Licences (/docs/concepts/licences)

## The code [#the-code]

All code (the engine, the bindings, the command line, the servers, the forge) is under the
[Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/blob/main/LICENSE): use it in open
and closed software alike, keep the notices.

## The data: two builds [#the-data-two-builds]

Every pack comes in one of two builds, built from the same schema with the same IDs:

| | Main build | Lite build |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | ODbL 1.0 | CC BY 4.0 |
| Sources | Open sources, OpenStreetMap included (no other share-alike, nothing non-commercial) | Only public-domain and attribution-only sources (clean room) |
| You must | Credit the sources; share improvements to the database you distribute | Credit the sources |
| Best for | The most complete data | Apps that cannot take on share-alike terms |

The lite build is **clean room**: its pipeline refuses share-alike, non-commercial and
proprietary sources at ingest, before any step reads them, and a licence gate fails a build
whose provenance includes one. The rules are in
[CLEAN_ROOM.md](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/blob/main/CLEAN_ROOM.md).

## You may keep it [#you-may-keep-it]

Commercial geocoding APIs limit how long you may store their answers. teigeodata's data is yours
to store, cache, ship inside apps and redistribute, under the build's licence. There are no
per-request terms and no keys.

## Attribution [#attribution]

Every pack carries the notices of its sources, and every answer can show them:

- `tgd inspect` lists a pack's notices, and `/packs` on the HTTP server returns them.
- Every HTTP and MCP answer carries an `attribution` (the `licence` field in Nominatim's
  format), built from the packs that answered.
- In an app, show the notices where you show the data, as you would map credits: an "About" or
  "Data sources" screen is usual. The world lite pack's notices today:

```text
Made with Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com), public domain
GeoNames (https://www.geonames.org), CC BY 4.0
Time zones: IANA Time Zone Database 2026f (public domain)
Wikidata (https://www.wikidata.org), CC0 1.0
Unicode CLDR (https://cldr.unicode.org), Copyright © 1991-2026 Unicode, Inc., under the Unicode License v3
Local Government Directory, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Government of India (https://lgdirectory.gov.in)
Administrative boundaries: Survey Department of Nepal and UN Resident Coordinator's Office in Nepal, via OCHA HDX (cod-ab-npl), CC BY-IGO 3.0
Elevation: NASADEM, NASA JPL and LP DAAC
Buildings: Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (https://cdla.dev/permissive-2-0/)
Buildings: Google Open Buildings v3 (Sirko et al. 2021, arXiv:2107.12283), CC BY 4.0
Central Bureau of Statistics (now National Statistics Office), Nepal, via Open Data Nepal (https://opendatanepal.com), Creative Commons Attribution
```

Credit the build's licence with them: each pack states it (`licence: "cc-by-4.0"` in
`tgd inspect` for a lite pack).

# Packs and components (/docs/concepts/packs)

A **pack** is one file (`.tgd`) of places and everything known about them: names, heights, the
hierarchy, boundaries, timezones, postal codes and the search index. Packs are built by the
forge from open sources, signed, and published in releases.

## Built to be mapped [#built-to-be-mapped]

A pack is laid out to be read where it lies: the engine memory-maps the file and reads the bytes
it needs, with no parsing step and no copy into the heap. Opening a 15 MB pack reads its head
(at most 16 KiB) and proves the block hashes of its large sections, and nothing else; a query touches only the pages it reads, which the operating
system shares between processes and drops under memory pressure.

- **Verified as it is read.** Every section carries a BLAKE3 hash in the head, and every 16 KiB
  block of a large section has its own. By default a section, or a block, is checked the first
  time a query reads it (`Verify::Lazy`); `Eager` checks everything when the pack opens.
- **Signed.** Released packs are signed with Ed25519 over the head, which holds every section's
  hash. `tgd verify --key` checks a signature; the store checks every pack it installs against
  the signed catalog. The data pre-releases published so far are not signed yet: check them by
  the SHA-256 their release lists, until the signing key is made for 1.0.
- **Forward compatible.** A reader skips sections it does not know, so older code keeps reading
  newer packs, and a pack states the oldest reader that can open it.

## Components [#components]

A pack is cut into **components**, each a set of sections. Install, download or link only the
ones your app uses; a query that needs a component you left out fails with `MissingComponent`
instead of answering wrongly.

| Component | What it holds | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `point` | IDs, coordinates, kinds, the spatial index and retired IDs | |
| `names` | Every name of every place | `point` |
| `search` | The name search index | `names` |
| `substring` | Search from three or more characters inside a word | `search` |
| `admin` | Parents, children and ISO 3166 codes | `point` |
| `boundaries` | The outlines of admin units, as shared arcs | `point` |
| `admin-index` | The admin units at any point | `boundaries` |
| `elevation` | Each place's height | `point` |
| `dem`, `dem-coarse` | Elevation grids: a country's terrain, and a coarse grid of the world | |
| `timezone` | Each place's timezone | `point`, `tz-rules` |
| `timezone-index` | The timezone at any point | `point`, `tz-rules` |
| `tz-rules` | The tzdb rules: offsets at any instant, local times | |
| `postal` | Postal codes, current and former | `point` |
| `extra` | Optional fields and cold data | `point` |

The world lite pack, by component (disk and compressed wire bytes, `data-2026.11.14.3`):

| Component | Disk | Wire | Download with what it needs |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| `point` | 1.60 MB | 1.06 MB | 1.06 MB |
| `elevation` | 0.32 MB | 0.23 MB | 1.29 MB |
| `admin` | 0.71 MB | 0.28 MB | 1.34 MB |
| `names` | 4.60 MB | 1.83 MB | 2.91 MB |
| `search` | 4.47 MB | 2.91 MB | 5.81 MB |
| `timezone` | 0.06 MB | 0.01 MB | 1.14 MB |
| `boundaries` | 2.19 MB | 2.03 MB | 3.11 MB |
| `admin-index` | 1.07 MB | 0.80 MB | 3.91 MB |
| `tz-rules` | 0.08 MB | 0.06 MB | 0.07 MB |
| `dem-coarse` | 0.53 MB | 0.52 MB | 0.52 MB |

So an app that only finds the nearest named place to a point needs `point` and `names`: 2.9 MB
on the wire instead of 9.8 MB. The libraries are cut the same way: each language's build can leave out the code of
components it does not use (the WebAssembly package has a smaller `-lookup` build without name
search).

A pack also splits **by language** (install the names of up to eight languages besides the base
names) and **by outline detail** (install a country's boundaries down to a level, simplified to
a tolerance in metres). `OpenOptions` and the store's install options take the same choices.

## Layers [#layers]

An engine answers from several packs at once; each is a **layer**. Where layers hold the same
place, one rule decides which answers: the higher `priority` you give, then the newer release,
then the more specific pack (a country over the world), then the pack's address as a last
tie-break, and the baseline always last. So a
detailed country pack overrides the world pack inside that country, while the world pack still
answers everywhere else. The answers do not depend on the order the packs were added (a CI gate
splits packs and compares). Typical stacks:

- **One world pack** bundled with the app: every country, its first-level units and its cities,
  and the full detail of the countries you serve.
- **A world baseline plus country packs** downloaded on demand: the user opens "Dubai", the
  app installs the UAE pack, and the engine answers from both.
- **Terrain packs** (`dem`) added over the coarse world grid where heights must be precise.

Layers can be added and removed while other threads query: each change publishes a new snapshot,
and queries already running finish on the one they started with.

## Where packs come from [#where-packs-come-from]

Today, packs are published as data pre-releases on GitHub, with checksums: download one and open
it. Once the signed catalog is live, the [store](/docs/concepts/store) finds, downloads, verifies
and updates packs for you.

# Places and IDs (/docs/concepts/places)

Everything teigeodata answers is about **places**. A place has:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | A stable ID, such as `tgd:np/1xhb`. |
| `name` | Its name in the pack's base language, with every other name it has (other scripts, languages, former and alternative names) behind it for search. |
| `kind` | What sort of place it is (below). |
| `level` | For an admin unit, its admin level; 0 for a country and for anything that is not a unit. |
| `lat`, `lon` | Its point in WGS84 degrees: the centre of a settlement, a label point for a unit. |
| `elevation` | Metres above mean sea level (EGM2008), with how it was found: `surveyed` from a source, `model` from the terrain. |
| `parent` | The ID of the smallest unit that holds it. |
| `tz` | Its IANA timezone. |
| `iso` | The ISO 3166 code of a country (`NP`) or a subdivision (`NP-P4`). |
| `population` | Its number of people, with where it came from: `stated` by a source (a census or an estimate), or `modelled` from a population grid over an admin unit. |

Any of these but the ID and point may be null where the data has no value; `kind` is null only
for a kind newer than the reader.

## Kinds [#kinds]

| Kind | What |
|---|---|
| `country` | A country. |
| `admin` | An admin unit: a province, a district, a municipality, a ward. Its `level` says which. |
| `settlement` | A city, town or village: where people live, whether or not it is a unit. |
| `locality` | A named part of a settlement: a neighbourhood, a tole, a chowk. |
| `natural` | A mountain, lake, river or other natural feature. |
| `postal_area` | The area of a postal code. |
| `timezone_area` | An area with one IANA timezone; its name is the zone. |

## Admin levels [#admin-levels]

Countries divide themselves differently, so each country's ladder is data: its
[profile](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/tree/main/data/countries) names each level.
Nepal's is country (0), province (1), district (2), local level (3, the municipality) and ward
(4). Code never assumes a ladder: ask for a place's `level` and its ancestors.

## IDs that last [#ids-that-last]

An ID is the country that first allocated it and a serial: `tgd:np/1xhb` is Nepal's serial
`1xhb` in base32. IDs are allocated once and never reused, so you can store them in your
database and look them up after any data update:

- A place keeps its ID through every rebuild, however its name, point or parent change.
- When two records turn out to be one place, the survivor keeps its ID and the other is
  **retired**: looking up a retired ID answers with the survivor.
- A place that moves to another country keeps the ID it was born with: the prefix is where the ID
  was allocated, not where the place is now.

`tgd:world/…` IDs belong to places in no country: oceans, seas, the world.

## Names in every script [#names-in-every-script]

A place carries every name the sources give it: its official name, names in other scripts and
languages, former names and common alternatives. Search reads all of them through a fold that
ignores case, accents and the small spelling differences of each script, and forgives typos,
so काठमाडौं, Kathmandu and Kathamandu all find the capital. Each country's spelling rules (such as
चोक written **Chowk**, not Chok) are data in its [lexicon](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/tree/main/data/countries),
each with its source.

# Results (/docs/concepts/results)

Every query of the bindings returns its rows as one **result blob**: a few bytes of header, then
each column stored contiguously. One blob crosses from the engine into your language in a single
copy, however many rows it holds, and a `Reader` reads it in place: whole columns as arrays with
no per-row work, or each row as your language's map or record.

```python
from teigeodata.blob import Reader

for place in Reader(engine.search("Pokhara", 3)):   # each row: a dict
    print(place["name"], place["lat"], place["lon"])

reader = Reader(engine.reverse(27.7172, 85.324, 100))  # whole columns, no per-row objects
lats, lons = reader.numbers("lat"), reader.numbers("lon")
```

## The same Reader everywhere [#the-same-reader-everywhere]

| | Rows and shape | A whole column | Each row |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | `reader.rows`, `reader.columns`, `has` | `numbers`, `strings`, `nulls`, `column` | iterate: `dict` |
| Node.js, WebAssembly | `rows`, `columns`, `has` | `numbers` (typed array), `strings`, `nulls`, `column` | iterate: object |
| Swift | `rows`, `columns`, `has` | `numbers`, `strings`, `nulls`, `column` | iterate: `Record` |
| Kotlin and Java | `rows()`, `columns()`, `has` | `numbers`, `strings`, `nulls`, `column` | iterate: `Map` |
| Dart | `rows`, `columns`, `has` | `numbers`, `strings`, `nulls`, `column` | iterate: `Map` |
| Go | `Rows()`, `Columns()`, `Has` | `Values[T]`, `Strings`, `Nulls`, `Column` | `Records()`: `map` |
| C | `tg_reader_init`, `tg_reader_find` | | `tg_reader_string`, `_number`, `_int`, `_is_null` |
| C++ | `rows()`, `columns()`, `has` | `numbers`, `strings`, `nulls`, `column` | iterate: `Row` |
| .NET | `Rows`, `Columns`, `Has` | `Values<T>` (span), `Strings`, `Nulls`, `Column` | iterate: dictionary |

Rust's typed engine returns `Place` values instead; `teigeodata-api` gives Rust the blobs too.

## Place columns [#place-columns]

Every query that returns places has these columns:

| Column | Type | Null when |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | never |
| `name` | string | the place has no name in the languages installed |
| `kind` | string | the place's kind is one this reader does not know (a newer pack) |
| `level` | integer | never (0 for anything that is not an admin unit) |
| `lat`, `lon` | number (degrees) | never |
| `elevation` | integer (metres, EGM2008) | no height is known |
| `parent` | string (an ID) | a root (a country, a timezone area), or a pack without the admin hierarchy |
| `tz` | string (an IANA zone) | the pack has no timezones there |
| `iso` | string (ISO 3166) | the place has no ISO code |
| `population` | integer (people) | no count is known, the place is a former unit, or the layer was installed without `extra` |
| `population_kind` | string: `stated` (a source's count) or `modelled` (a population grid over an admin unit) | as `population` |

and some queries add their own:

| Query | Added columns |
|---|---|
| `search`, `search_with` | `score`: compares the rows of one query only |
| `reverse`, `within_radius`, `nearby` | `meters` (great-circle distance), `bearing` (degrees clockwise from north, from the place to the point) |
| postal queries | `postal`, `scheme`, `code_kind`, `valid_from`, `valid_to` |

Queries that do not return places have their own columns: `elevation_at` (`meters`, `source`,
`resolution_m`, `datum`), `tz_offset_at` (`seconds`, `dst`, `abbr`), `tz_local` (`kind`,
`before`, `after`), `tz_zones` (`zone`), `distance` (`meters`, `bearing`), `boundary` (`id`,
`lod`, `tolerance_m`, `vertices`, `geojson`). The [reference](/docs/reference) lists every query.

## Nulls, numbers and strings [#nulls-numbers-and-strings]

- **Null is not zero.** A whole number column reads a null row as zero; check `nulls(column)`
  (or read rows, where nulls are your language's null) before trusting a 0.
- **Numbers keep their type.** A column is stored as 8, 16, 32 or 64-bit integers or 32 or
  64-bit floats; the readers give each in the language's natural type. 64-bit integers are exact
  to 2^53 where a language has only doubles (JavaScript).
- **Strings are UTF-8,** stored once per distinct value where a column repeats (`kind`, `tz`):
  reading them costs a lookup, not a decode per row.

## The format [#the-format]

A blob starts with the magic `TGB1`, the row count, the column count and the total length (16
bytes), then one 40-byte descriptor per column: its name, type, where its values are, where its
strings or dictionary are, and where its null bitmap is. Every offset is checked when the reader
is made, so no read can leave the blob, even for bytes from an untrusted source. The format is
specified in [bindings](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/blob/main/docs/04-architecture/bindings.md)
and tested in every language against the same fixtures, including malformed blobs each reader
must refuse.

# The store (/docs/concepts/store)

The **store** keeps the packs installed on a device and the signed **catalog** that says which
packs exist. It is how an app downloads data when a user needs it: the user searches for
"Dubai", the app finds that the UAE pack holds it, installs that pack, and from then on answers
offline.

<Callout type="warn" title="The catalog is not live yet">
The store is built and tested, but the signed catalog it reads goes live with the first catalog
release, after the offline key ceremony. Until then, data comes as GitHub pre-releases:
download a pack, check its SHA-256, and open it with `open_file`.
</Callout>

## What it does [#what-it-does]

- **Finds packs offline.** `find` takes a name and returns the places it matches with the
  catalog's packs that hold each one; `locate` does the same for the countries at a point. Both
  read the stored catalog alone, so the app can offer the download, with its size, before it has
a network.
- **Installs a part.** Install a pack whole, or some components, the names of some languages,
  and boundaries down to a level: the same choices as in [packs](/docs/concepts/packs).
- **Verifies every byte.** The catalog is signed metadata (TUF): every pack it lists has its
  head's hash, the head holds every section's hash, and large sections hold a hash per 16 KiB
  block. Nothing is written before it is checked against that chain, so a bad mirror or a broken
  download is refused and the next mirror resumes.
- **Survives crashes.** An install that a crash or a kill cuts short is finished or undone the
  next time the store opens; the installed packs are never half-written.
- **Updates and evicts.** `update` moves installed packs to the catalog's releases, keeping the
  components and languages installed. Pinned packs are kept when room is made; `remove` takes a
  pack out with the dependencies nothing else needs.
- **Gives you an engine.** `engine()` opens every installed pack, with the parts installed.

## In code [#in-code]

The store's calls block on the network and the disk, so call them off the UI thread or use the
language's asynchronous form (`…Async` in Swift, Kotlin and Java, Dart, Node.js and .NET; `aio`
in Python). An install runs as a `Job` that reports its bytes as it goes and can be cancelled:
cancelled, it leaves the store as it was.

```python
import teigeodata
from teigeodata import aio

store = teigeodata.Store.open(path)  # set up once with Store.create
job = store.install("ae", teigeodata.InstallOptions(components="point,names,search"))
async for done, total in aio.progress(job):
    print(f"{done} of {total} bytes")
await aio.result(job)                  # raises the job's error, if any
engine = store.engine()                # every installed pack, opened
```

On iOS and Android a download may need to go on while the app is suspended. `install_pass`
splits an install so the platform's own download service fetches the bytes (a background
`URLSession`, `WorkManager`): each pass lists the byte ranges still missing, the platform fetches
them into files, and the next pass verifies and installs what arrived.

## From the command line [#from-the-command-line]

`tgd init`, `refresh`, `catalog`, `find`, `locate`, `install`, `update`, `remove`, `pin`,
`status` and `repair` do the same from a shell; see the [command line](/docs/cli#the-store).
`tgd serve` and `tgd mcp` follow the store: a pack installed or updated while they run is
answered from within seconds.

# Coverage (/docs/data/coverage)

<Callout title="Generated from the data">
This page is written by `cargo xtask data-pages` from `data/countries/` and the pack the site's
examples run on (`world-np-lite.tgd`, data release `data-2026.11.14.3`), and CI fails when it differs. It changes with
each release.
</Callout>

`world-np-lite.tgd` holds **172,339 places**: 171,962 in 248 countries and territories, and 377 timezone areas. Countries with rules of their own in
[`data/countries`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/tree/main/data/countries) have a
page of their own; the rest are covered by the world sources alone.

## Inside the pack [#inside-the-pack]

| Component | Bytes |
|---|--:|
| head, seek table, block hashes | 23,792 |
| `admin` | 705,560 |
| `admin-index` | 1,069,672 |
| `boundaries` | 2,190,508 |
| `dem-coarse` | 526,240 |
| `elevation` | 315,180 |
| `names` | 4,599,148 |
| `point` | 1,597,508 |
| `search` | 4,472,092 |
| `timezone` | 55,404 |
| `tz-rules` | 83,320 |
| **the file**, with the alignment between sections | **15,641,408** |

What each component answers is in [packs](/docs/concepts/packs#components).

# Data (/docs/data)

Coverage grows by data releases: Nepal first, then India, South Asia, Asia, the USA and the rest
of the world. Every release is built from a commit on `main`, keeps every published ID, and
lists its checksums.

## The latest release: data-2026.11.14.3 [#the-latest-release-data-202611143]

| File | What | Places | Disk | Wire |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| [`world-np-lite.tgd`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/releases/download/data-2026.11.14.3/world-np-lite.tgd) | The world's countries, first-level units and cities of 5,000 or more; India's districts and statutory towns; Nepal in full. Names in Nepali, Hindi and English. | 172,339 | 15.6 MB | 9.8 MB |
| [`baseline-lite.tgd`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/releases/download/data-2026.11.14.3/baseline-lite.tgd) | The baseline to ship in an app: countries, first-level units, cities of 15,000 or more. | | 5.0 MB | |
| [`points-en-lite.tgd`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/releases/download/data-2026.11.14.3/points-en-lite.tgd) | The baseline's points and English names alone. | | 1.9 MB | |

All three are the **lite build** (CC BY 4.0). Check them with the release's `SHA256SUMS`:

```sh
shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
```

The release notes and each file's summary are on the
[release page](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/releases/tag/data-2026.11.14.3).

### Inside world-np-lite.tgd [#inside-world-np-litetgd]

Every component's bytes, and every country's places by kind and admin level, are on the
[coverage page](/docs/data/coverage), read from the pack itself.

Places with a name in each language:

| Places | Rows | Nepali | Hindi | English |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Nepal | 95,715 | 99.9% | 0.4% | 0.3% |
| The rest of the world | 76,247 | 2.7% | 20.2% | 12.7% |

## Countries [#countries]

| Country | Today | Levels |
|---|---|---|
| [Nepal](/docs/data/countries/np) | In full: provinces, districts and local levels with their boundaries, the provinces' ISO codes, wards, about 90,000 settlements, localities (toles, chowks) and natural features (peaks, passes), every one with a height. | country, province, district, local level, ward |
| [India](/docs/data/countries/in) | Districts and statutory towns, with the states' current ISO codes. Full coverage is next. | country, state, district |
| Every other country | The country, its first-level units with ISO codes and boundaries, and its cities of 5,000 or more. | country, first level |

Every country, with its places by kind and level, is on the [coverage page](/docs/data/coverage).
Each country's rules (its admin ladder, the spellings of its generic terms, its sources and its
perspective on borders) are data in
[`data/countries`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/tree/main/data/countries), each rule
with its source.

## Sources [#sources]

The lite build reads only public-domain and attribution-only sources:

| Source | What it gives | Licence |
|---|---|---|
| Natural Earth | Country and first-level outlines | Public domain |
| GeoNames | Cities and settlements, alternative names | CC BY 4.0 |
| Wikidata | Nepal's places and their links between sources; the world's names in Nepali and Hindi with English aliases; ISO codes; units' populations | CC0 1.0 |
| IANA tz database | Timezones and their rules | Public domain |
| Unicode CLDR | Current ISO 3166 subdivision codes | Unicode License v3 |
| OCHA HDX COD-AB (Nepal) | Nepal's provinces, districts and local levels | CC BY-IGO 3.0 |
| Nepal's Central Bureau of Statistics, via Open Data Nepal | Codes and Nepali names | Creative Commons Attribution |
| India's Local Government Directory | India's districts and towns | Free reproduction with acknowledgement |
| NASADEM | Terrain heights | Public domain (NASA) |
| Microsoft and Google building footprints | Where settlements' cores are | CDLA-Permissive 2.0, CC BY 4.0 |

The main build adds OpenStreetMap (ODbL), Overture's divisions for the world's countries and
first-level units (ODbL), timezone-boundary-builder's zone outlines (ODbL), WorldPop's modelled
populations (CC BY 4.0, kept to the main build) and Copernicus GLO-30 heights. Every source is pinned
by version and SHA-256, and every pack lists the notices of the sources it was built from: see
[licences](/docs/concepts/licences).

# Measured (/docs/data/measured)

<Callout title="Generated from the gates">
This page is written by `cargo xtask data-pages` from the records in
[`site/data/measured`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/tree/main/site/data/measured), each
written by the gate that measured it (`--record`). Every figure says when, where and at which
commit it was measured: compare a timing only with timings from the same machine, and read one
from a busy machine (a high load average) as a ceiling, not a typical value.
</Callout>

The bytes of each component of the released pack are on the [coverage page](/docs/data/coverage);
how good the data is, and how it is gated, is on [accuracy](/docs/concepts/accuracy).

## WebAssembly packages [#webassembly-packages]

Each npm package's module after `wasm-opt -Oz`, raw and gzipped at level 9. `cargo xtask package-wasm` fails a build whose gzipped module is over its budget.

Measured 2026-11-15 on Darwin arm64, 10 cores (load average 10.36), commit [`25ad7e5`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/commit/25ad7e5), by `cargo xtask package-wasm --record`.

| Package | Holds | Module | gzip -9 | Budget | Headroom |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `teigeodata-wasm` | every component | 605118 B | 253910 B | 262144 B | 3.1% |
| `teigeodata-wasm-lookup` | every query at a point or by ID | 380167 B | 145724 B | 153600 B | 5.1% |

## Library bytes per feature set [#library-bytes-per-feature-set]

What each feature set of the runtime crates adds to a linked library (`tools/size-probe`, a baseline that any host library links subtracted), natively in the release profile and for wasm32 in the size profile.

Measured 2026-11-15 on Darwin arm64, 10 cores (load average 7.04), commit [`25ad7e5`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/commit/25ad7e5), by `cargo xtask sizes --record`.

| Feature set | native B | native gzip | wasm32 B | wasm32 gzip |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| open: head checks, section lookup | 16.4 KiB | 12.3 KiB | 18.4 KiB | 8.4 KiB |
| open + BLAKE3 of every section | 16.5 KiB | 13.5 KiB | 20.2 KiB | 9.2 KiB |
| open + Ed25519 signature check | 32.7 KiB | 27.8 KiB | 47.6 KiB | 20.0 KiB |
| open + every section view (places, hierarchy, ID map, names, components) | 64.9 KiB | 36.7 KiB | 103.5 KiB | 25.8 KiB |
| open + BLOBS (`ruzstd`) | 65.0 KiB | 43.3 KiB | 124.0 KiB | 34.5 KiB |
| the whole reader: all of the above | 129.7 KiB | 74.1 KiB | 171.8 KiB | 53.6 KiB |
| the writer alone (forge side) | 16.5 KiB | 16.3 KiB | 26.1 KiB | 11.2 KiB |
| the engine, points only: open, `get`, `reverse` | 113.5 KiB | 67.7 KiB | 143.4 KiB | 43.8 KiB |
| the engine, every query | 452.4 KiB | 248.1 KiB | 459.8 KiB | 184.1 KiB |

Baseline (subtracted): native 278.5 KiB, wasm32 16.1 KiB.

## Scaling across threads [#scaling-across-threads]

Throughput of one shared engine on `np-places-lite.tgd`: each thread takes the current snapshot for every query, as a server's handlers do, and runs `get`, `reverse` (10 nearest), `admin_at`, `tz_at` and `search` (10 hits) in turn. The best of three rounds per thread count. The gate fails when four threads reach less than 1.5× one thread, the mark of a lock on the query path; the machine is shared and mixes performance and efficiency cores, so the figures are a floor.

Measured 2026-11-15 on Darwin arm64, 10 cores (load average 6.54), commit [`668ec58`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/commit/668ec58), by `cargo xtask scaling np-places-lite.tgd --record`.

| Threads | Queries/s | Speed-up | Efficiency |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 207739 | 1.00× | 100% |
| 2 | 416120 | 2.00× | 100% |
| 4 | 811143 | 3.90× | 98% |
| 8 | 1267633 | 6.10× | 76% |

## Server load [#server-load]

`tgd serve` on loopback, each route driven by oha 1.17.0 for 5 s at each point, twice; round two is reported, and the footprint's growth across it is the leak check. `tools/load/budget.toml` sets each point's floor and ceiling.

Measured 2026-11-15 on Darwin arm64, 10 cores (load average 22.79), commit [`3688d14`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/commit/3688d14), by `cargo xtask load <pack> --check tools/load/budget.toml --record`.

**np-places-lite**

| Route | c | req/s | p50 ms | p99 ms | requests | failed |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| search | 1 | 4793 | 0.134 | 1.843 | 23979 | 0 |
| search | 16 | 64215 | 0.191 | 1.054 | 321181 | 0 |
| search | 64 | 61182 | 0.913 | 3.390 | 306084 | 0 |
| reverse | 16 | 71036 | 0.174 | 1.007 | 355321 | 0 |
| get | 16 | 84291 | 0.154 | 0.800 | 421732 | 0 |
| near | 16 | 63304 | 0.194 | 1.110 | 316628 | 0 |
| hierarchy | 16 | 90183 | 0.157 | 0.530 | 451085 | 0 |
| boundary | 16 | 8875 | 1.551 | 8.369 | 44374 | 0 |
| nominatim | 16 | 53444 | 0.256 | 1.011 | 267380 | 0 |
| mcp search | 16 | 39315 | 0.370 | 1.216 | 196674 | 0 |

footprint: 5616 KB idle, 16384 KB peak, -3072 KB across round two

**world-baseline-lite**

| Route | c | req/s | p50 ms | p99 ms | requests | failed |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| search | 1 | 4129 | 0.103 | 1.951 | 20649 | 0 |
| search | 16 | 73481 | 0.162 | 0.928 | 367581 | 0 |
| search | 64 | 81055 | 0.676 | 2.875 | 405502 | 0 |
| reverse | 16 | 58112 | 0.187 | 1.325 | 290656 | 0 |
| get | 16 | 78654 | 0.149 | 0.930 | 393402 | 0 |
| near | 16 | 53536 | 0.190 | 1.495 | 267787 | 0 |
| hierarchy | 16 | 82638 | 0.142 | 0.950 | 413413 | 0 |
| boundary | 16 | 31980 | 0.301 | 3.029 | 159944 | 0 |
| nominatim | 16 | 69888 | 0.172 | 1.029 | 349665 | 0 |
| mcp search | 16 | 42750 | 0.292 | 1.498 | 213764 | 0 |

footprint: 5072 KB idle, 10240 KB peak, +0 KB across round two

## Phone-class estimates [#phone-class-estimates]

The phone-class bench (P1, G-phone) on `world-np-lite.tgd`: open, the first query of each kind, search a keystroke at a time and the point queries, each the minimum of several rounds here and multiplied by 6.5 (this machine's core over a low-end phone's), and the heap counted by allocator; the gate fails when an estimate is over its target. A point query is `reverse_in_country` (10 nearest), `admin_at`, `tz_at` and `elevation_at`; the page cache is warm, as on a relaunch.

Measured 2026-11-15 on Darwin arm64, 10 cores (load average 7.63), commit [`41ba69a`](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/commit/41ba69a), by `cargo xtask phone world-np-lite.tgd --record`.

| Measure | Here | Phone estimate | Target |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| open | 133.75µs | 869.38µs | 50ms |
| first queries | 6.06ms | 39.40ms | 150ms |
|   first get | 809.79µs | 5.26ms | – |
|   first reverse | 2.21ms | 14.39ms | – |
|   first admin_at | 458.00ns | 2.98µs | – |
|   first tz_at | 31.62µs | 205.56µs | – |
|   first elevation_at | 286.42µs | 1.86ms | – |
|   first search | 2.57ms | 16.68ms | – |
| keystroke p50 | 9.25µs | 60.12µs | – |
| keystroke p99 | 203.46µs | 1.32ms | 16ms |
| keystroke max | 235.00µs | 1.53ms | 50ms |
| point query p99 | 76.00µs | 494.00µs | 2ms |
| get p99 | 250.00ns | 1.62µs | 500µs |
| derive SUBSTRING | 389.03ms | 2.53s | 3s |
| heap after open and the first queries | 0.05 MiB | | 4 MiB |
| heap peak | 0.05 MiB | | 16 MiB |
| heap peak while deriving SUBSTRING | 55.00 MiB | | 64 MiB |

# Quickstart (/docs/getting-started)

This page takes you from nothing to answers in a few minutes: a pack, the `tgd` command line to
look inside it, and the same queries from code.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Get a pack [#get-a-pack]

A pack is one file. The world lite pack holds the world's countries, first-level units and
cities of 5,000 or more, India's districts and statutory towns, and Nepal in full: 172,339
places named in Nepali, Hindi and English, with heights, admin units, timezones and boundaries.

```sh
curl -LO https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/releases/download/data-2026.11.14.3/world-np-lite.tgd
shasum -a 256 world-np-lite.tgd
# 243ae55509a538b1f61da50994a791cc78e7deb70bb4bf743b9f59d458cbe3f3  world-np-lite.tgd
```

It is 15.6 MB on disk and 9.8 MB compressed on the wire, under CC BY 4.0: you may ship it in an
app, with the credits it carries.
</Step>

<Step>
### Install the command line [#install-the-command-line]

`tgd` inspects, verifies and queries packs, and serves them over HTTP and MCP. Install it from
crates.io (a Rust toolchain is all it needs):

```sh
cargo install --locked teigeodata-cli
```
</Step>

<Step>
### Ask it something [#ask-it-something]

```sh title="Search"
tgd search Pokhara -k 3 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Pokhara  settlement  28.266890,83.968000  tgd:np/1xhb  1006 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 132
Pokhara  admin 3  28.209407,83.981817  tgd:np/1xnr  842 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 105
Pokhara  settlement  28.063631,82.378569  tgd:np/15t1  612 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu  score 90
```

The first is the city (a settlement), the second the metropolitan municipality that holds it
(an admin unit at level 3), the third a smaller settlement of the same name farther west. `tgd:np/1xhb` is
the city's stable ID. From a point:

```sh title="Admin units at a point"
tgd admin 28.2096 83.9856 --pack "$PACK"
```

```text title="Output"
Nepal  country NP  28.000000,84.000000  tgd:np/1wmc  1046 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
Gandaki  admin 1 NP-P4  28.384514,84.035774  tgd:np/2922  2689 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
Kaski  admin 2  28.345513,83.970886  tgd:np/295c  1231 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
Pokhara  admin 3  28.209407,83.981817  tgd:np/1xnr  842 m (model)  Asia/Kathmandu
```

The [command-line guide](/docs/cli) shows every query.
</Step>

<Step>
### Use it from code [#use-it-from-code]

[Install the package for your language](/docs/getting-started/install), then follow the
guides, which open this same pack and run every query with its output in each language:

<Cards>
<Card title="Open a pack" href="/docs/guides/open" />

<Card title="Search by name" href="/docs/guides/search" />

<Card title="Reverse geocoding" href="/docs/guides/reverse" />

<Card title="Timezones" href="/docs/guides/timezones" />
</Cards>

The search above, from code:

<Tabs groupId="lang" persist items={["Rust","Python","Node.js","Browser","Swift","Kotlin","Java","Dart","Go","C","C++","C#"]}>
<Tab value="Rust">
```rust title="tour.rs"
engine.search_with(
    "Pokhara",
    3,
    &SearchOptions::default(),
    &mut scratch,
    &mut hits,
)?;
for hit in &hits {
    let p = describe(&engine, &hit.place)?;
    println!(
        "{}  {}  {}  {:.4}, {:.4}  score {}",
        p.id, p.name, p.kind, p.lat, p.lon, hit.score
    );
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Python">
```python title="tour.py"
for p in rows(engine.search("Pokhara", 3)):
    print(f"{p['id']}  {p['name']}  {p['kind']}  {p['lat']:.4f}, {p['lon']:.4f}  score {p['score']}")
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Node.js">
```js title="tour.mjs"
for (const p of new Reader(engine.search("Pokhara", 3))) {
  console.log(`${p.id}  ${p.name}  ${p.kind}  ${fixed(p.lat, 4)}, ${fixed(p.lon, 4)}  score ${p.score}`);
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Browser">
```js title="tour.mjs"
for (const p of new Reader(engine.search("Pokhara", 3))) {
  console.log(`${p.id}  ${p.name}  ${p.kind}  ${fixed(p.lat, 4)}, ${fixed(p.lon, 4)}  score ${p.score}`);
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Swift">
```swift title="main.swift"
for p in try Reader(engine.search("Pokhara", limit: 3)) {
    print("\(p["id"]!)  \(p["name"]!)  \(p["kind"]!)  \(fixed(p.double("lat"), 4)), \(fixed(p.double("lon"), 4))  score \(p["score"]!)")
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Kotlin">
```kotlin title="Tour.kt"
for (p in Reader(engine.search("Pokhara", 3))) {
    println("%s  %s  %s  %.4f, %.4f  score %d".f(p["id"], p["name"], p["kind"], p["lat"], p["lon"], p["score"]))
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Java">
```java title="Tour.java"
for (Map<String, Object> p : new Reader(engine.search("Pokhara", 3))) {
    System.out.println(f("%s  %s  %s  %.4f, %.4f  score %d",
            p.get("id"), p.get("name"), p.get("kind"), p.get("lat"), p.get("lon"), p.get("score")));
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Dart">
```dart title="tour.dart"
for (final p in Reader(engine.search('Pokhara', 3))) {
  final (lat, lon) = (p['lat'] as double, p['lon'] as double);
  print(
    '${p['id']}  ${p['name']}  ${p['kind']}  ${lat.toStringAsFixed(4)}, '
    '${lon.toStringAsFixed(4)}  score ${p['score']}',
  );
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Go">
```go title="tour.go"
for _, p := range rows(engine.Search("Pokhara", 3)) {
	fmt.Printf("%s  %s  %s  %.4f, %.4f  score %d\n",
		p["id"], p["name"], p["kind"], p["lat"], p["lon"], p["score"])
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="C">
```c title="tour.c"
r = reader(tg_engine_search(engine, TEXT("Pokhara"), 3, &blob), &blob);
for (uint32_t i = 0; i < r.rows; i++) {
    printf("%.*s  %.*s  %.*s  %.4f, %.4f  score %lld\n", S(&r, "id", i), S(&r, "name", i), S(&r, "kind", i),
           num(&r, "lat", i), num(&r, "lon", i), integer(&r, "score", i));
}
tg_bytes_free(blob);
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="C++">
```cpp title="tour.cpp"
const tg::Blob hits = engine.search("Pokhara", 3);
for (auto p : tg::Reader(hits)) {
    std::cout << *p.string("id") << "  " << *p.string("name") << "  " << *p.string("kind") << "  "
              << fixed(p.number("lat"), 4) << ", " << fixed(p.number("lon"), 4) << "  score "
              << *p.integer("score") << '\n';
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="C#">
```csharp title="Program.cs"
foreach (var p in new BlobReader(engine.Search("Pokhara", 3)))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{p["id"]}  {p["name"]}  {p["kind"]}  {p["lat"]:F4}, {p["lon"]:F4}  score {p["score"]}");
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>
</Step>
</Steps>

## What to read next [#what-to-read-next]

- [Places and IDs](/docs/concepts/places): what a place is, its kinds and levels, and why IDs
  stay stable.
- [Packs and components](/docs/concepts/packs): what is inside a pack and how to ship only the
  parts you use.
- [Results](/docs/concepts/results): the columns every query returns and how to read them fast.
- [Licences](/docs/concepts/licences): what you must credit, and where.

# Install (/docs/getting-started/install)

teigeodata is one Rust engine with a binding for each language, generated from one
definition: the calls, their arguments and the columns they return are the same everywhere.
Pick your language; every page of these docs remembers it.

## Add the package [#add-the-package]

<Tabs groupId="lang" persist items={["Rust","Python","Node.js","Browser","Swift","Kotlin","Java","Dart","Go","C","C++","C#"]}>
<Tab value="Rust">
teigeodata is written in Rust, and Rust gets the engine itself: typed places, typed IDs and
points, and queries that write into buffers you reuse, so a warm query allocates nothing. Every
other language reaches the same engine through a generated binding.

```sh
cargo add teigeodata-core teigeodata-engine
```

The crates on crates.io: `teigeodata-core`, `-engine`, `-sync` (the store), `-api`, `-server`,
`-cli` (`tgd`) and what they need, all at the same version.

The minimum Rust version is the one `rust-toolchain.toml` pins. `teigeodata-engine`'s default
features read packs from files (`mmap`); `teigeodata-sync` adds the store (download, verify,
update); the core crates build for `no_std` targets.
</Tab>

<Tab value="Python">
The Python package is a native extension (PyO3) over the Rust engine, with type stubs. One
`abi3` wheel per platform serves CPython 3.11 and later; free-threaded builds (3.14t, 3.15t) get
their own wheels and run queries in parallel without the GIL.

<Tabs items={["PyPI","From a checkout"]}>
<Tab value="PyPI">
```sh
pip install teigeodata
```

Wheels for Linux (glibc and musl), macOS and Windows on x64 and Arm64.
</Tab>

<Tab value="From a checkout">
To build from a checkout instead (a Rust toolchain is all it needs;
`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata && cd teigeodata
git checkout v1.1.0
PYO3_BUILD_EXTENSION_MODULE=1 cargo build --release -p teigeodata-python --manifest-path bindings/Cargo.toml
cp bindings/target/release/libteigeodata_python.so bindings/python/teigeodata/_native.abi3.so   # .dylib on macOS
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/bindings/python
```

Or build a wheel with [maturin](https://www.maturin.rs): `pip install ./bindings/python`.
</Tab>
</Tabs>
</Tab>

<Tab value="Node.js">
`teigeodata` is a native addon (N-API, napi-rs layout) with TypeScript types: one
prebuilt addon per platform, installed as an optional dependency, so `npm install` downloads only
yours. It runs on Node.js, and on Bun and Deno through their N-API support. For browsers and
edge workers use the WebAssembly package (the **Browser** tab), which has the same API.

<Tabs items={["npm","From a checkout"]}>
<Tab value="npm">
```sh
npm install teigeodata
```

npm installs the native addon for your platform with it (`@teispace/teigeodata-<platform>`).
</Tab>

<Tab value="From a checkout">
To build from a checkout instead (a Rust toolchain is all it needs;
`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata && cd teigeodata
git checkout v1.1.0
cargo build --release -p teigeodata-node --manifest-path bindings/Cargo.toml
cp bindings/target/release/libteigeodata_node.so bindings/node/teigeodata.node   # .dylib on macOS
npm install ./bindings/node
```

`cargo xtask package-node` makes the packages as they are published, under `target/node/`.
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Node.js 22 or later. The package is ESM and CommonJS (`require` works too).
</Tab>

<Tab value="Browser">
`teigeodata-wasm` is the engine compiled to WebAssembly, for browsers, Web Workers,
Deno, Bun, Node.js and Cloudflare Workers. The API is the Node.js package's (the **Node.js** tab);
the difference is where packs come from: a page has no file system, so it opens a pack from its
bytes. After that one download, every query runs locally. The [playground](/playground) is this
package in a page: every query on the pack below, with the code each answer came from.

<Tabs items={["npm","From a checkout"]}>
<Tab value="npm">
```sh
npm install teigeodata-wasm          # every component
npm install teigeodata-wasm-lookup   # no name search: a smaller module
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="From a checkout">
To build from a checkout instead (a Rust toolchain is all it needs;
`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata && cd teigeodata
git checkout v1.1.0
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --version 0.2.130 --locked
cargo xtask package-wasm          # needs binaryen's wasm-opt; writes target/wasm/full/
npm install ./target/wasm/full
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Two packages, the same API. The full module is at most 256 KiB gzipped (a CI gate); the
`-lookup` one leaves out name search and is at most 150 KiB, for apps that only reverse geocode,
read timezones or look places up by ID.
</Tab>

<Tab value="Swift">
The Swift package wraps the C library: on Apple platforms it links an XCFramework (iOS,
the iOS simulators, macOS), on Linux the library you build. Swift 6 with typed throws; every
handle is `Sendable`.

<Tabs items={["Swift Package Manager","From a checkout"]}>
<Tab value="Swift Package Manager">
The release tags are the Swift releases; each one fetches the release's XCFramework and checks
its checksum:

```swift title="Package.swift"
dependencies: [
    .package(url: "https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata", from: "1.1.0"),
],
targets: [
    .target(name: "MyApp", dependencies: [.product(name: "TeiGeodata", package: "teigeodata")]),
]
```

In Xcode: File › Add Package Dependencies, and the repository URL.
</Tab>

<Tab value="From a checkout">
To build from a checkout instead (a Rust toolchain is all it needs;
`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata && cd teigeodata
git checkout v1.1.0
cargo build --release -p teigeodata-ffi        # the C library the package links
```

and depend on `bindings/swift` by path, linking `target/release` as the tour's
[Package.swift](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/blob/main/site/examples/swift/Tour/Package.swift)
does. `cargo xtask package-swift` makes the XCFramework the release ships.
</Tab>
</Tabs>

iOS 15, macOS 12, and Linux.
</Tab>

<Tab value="Kotlin">
One library serves Kotlin and Java, on desktop JVMs (Java 17 or later) and on Android (API 24
or later). It calls the native library through JNI; the JAR carries it for each desktop
platform, the AAR for each Android ABI (arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86_64, 16 KB page aligned).

<Tabs items={["Gradle","From a checkout"]}>
<Tab value="Gradle">
On Maven Central:

```kotlin title="build.gradle.kts"
dependencies {
    implementation("com.teispace:teigeodata:1.1.0")            // desktop JVM
    // implementation("com.teispace:teigeodata-android:1.1.0") // Android
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="From a checkout">
To build from a checkout instead (a Rust toolchain is all it needs;
`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata && cd teigeodata
git checkout v1.1.0
cargo xtask package-jvm --desktop         # target/jvm/teigeodata-<version>.jar
cargo xtask package-jvm --android         # target/jvm/teigeodata-<version>.aar (needs the NDK)
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>
</Tab>

One library serves Kotlin and Java, on desktop JVMs (Java 17 or later) and on Android (API 24

platform, the AAR for each Android ABI (arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86_64, 16 KB page aligned).

<Tab value="Dart">
One package for Dart and Flutter on Android, iOS, macOS, Linux, Windows and the web. Natively
it calls the C library through FFI, supplied by the package's build hook; on the web (dart2js or
dart2wasm) the same classes run on the WebAssembly module.

<Tabs items={["pub.dev","From the repository"]}>
<Tab value="pub.dev">
```sh
dart pub add teigeodata      # or: flutter pub add teigeodata
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="From the repository">
```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
dependencies:
  teigeodata:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata
      ref: v1.1.0
      path: bindings/dart
```

To build the library with cargo instead of downloading it, point the build hook at a checkout:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
hooks:
  user_defines:
    teigeodata:
      source: path/to/teigeodata
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Dart 3.10 or later (Flutter 3.38 or later). The build hook fetches the prebuilt library for the
target and checks it against the SHA-256 the package pins; `library:` names one you built,
`prebuilt_base:` a mirror.
</Tab>

<Tab value="Go">
The Go module calls the C library through cgo, or through
[purego](https://github.com/ebitengine/purego) when built with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, so it cross-compiles
without a C toolchain. The library is loaded at run time: the file passed to `LoadLibrary`, then
the one `TEIGEODATA_LIB` names, then the release's prebuilt library in the user cache (checked
against the SHA-256 the module pins), then the system's.

```sh
go get github.com/teispace/teigeodata/bindings/go
```

The module's versions are the tags `bindings/go/vX.Y.Z`, made with each release. Go 1.26 or
later. Fetch the release's prebuilt library once:

```sh
go run github.com/teispace/teigeodata/bindings/go/cmd/teigeodata-fetch
```

or build it from a checkout and name it:

```sh
cargo build --release -p teigeodata-ffi
export TEIGEODATA_LIB=$PWD/target/release/libteigeodata_ffi.so   # .dylib on macOS, .dll on Windows
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="C">
The C library is the ABI every other binding builds on: plain functions, opaque handles,
status codes, and no global state but each thread's last error. Its header is checked against the
last release's on every change, so a minor release never breaks a program built against it.

<Tabs items={["Release package","From a checkout"]}>
<Tab value="Release package">
From the [release](https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/releases/latest): unpack `teigeodata-c-<version>-<target>.tar.gz`, which holds the headers,
the shared and static libraries, a pkg-config file and a CMake package.

```sh
cc tour.c $(pkg-config --cflags --libs teigeodata) -o tour
```

```cmake title="CMakeLists.txt"
find_package(teigeodata REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(tour PRIVATE teigeodata::teigeodata)
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="From a checkout">
To build from a checkout instead (a Rust toolchain is all it needs;
`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata && cd teigeodata
git checkout v1.1.0
cargo xtask package-c        # target/package/teigeodata-c-<version>-<target>/
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>
</Tab>

<Tab value="C++">
`teigeodata.hpp` is a header-only C++17 layer over the C library: RAII handles, `std::string_view`
arguments, exceptions with the stable error codes, and `teigeodata_reader.hpp` to read results
with a range-based `for`. Everything is in namespace `teigeodata`; the tour shortens it with
`namespace tg = teigeodata;`.

Install the C package (the **C** tab): the C++ headers ship in it. Then
compile as C++17 or later:

```sh
c++ -std=c++17 tour.cpp $(pkg-config --cflags --libs teigeodata) -o tour
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="C#">
`Teispace.TeiGeodata` is the .NET binding: source-generated P/Invoke (`LibraryImport`) with
no marshalling at run time, compatible with NativeAOT and trimming. The package carries the
native library for Windows, macOS and Linux (glibc and musl) on x64 and Arm64.

<Tabs items={["From a checkout","NuGet"]}>
<Tab value="NuGet">
Not on NuGet yet. Once it is:

```sh

```
</Tab>

<Tab value="From a checkout">

`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the version):

