
```js title="MapLibre"
map.addSource("admin", { type: "geojson", data: `${server}/v1/admin?lat=28.2096&lon=83.9856&format=geojson` });
map.addLayer({ id: "admin", type: "circle", source: "admin" });
```

## Nominatim-compatible [#nominatim-compatible]

`/search`, `/reverse` and `/lookup` speak Nominatim's API for the parameters its clients use,
in the `json`, `jsonv2` and `geojson` formats (JSONP is refused: use CORS):

| Route | Parameters |
|---|---|
| `/search` | `q`, or the structured `amenity`, `street`, `city`, `county`, `state`, `country`, `postalcode`; `limit` (at most 40, as Nominatim); `countrycodes`; `viewbox` and `bounded`; `addressdetails` |
| `/reverse` | `lat`, `lon`, `zoom` (how coarse a place to answer); `addressdetails` (on by default) |
| `/lookup` | `osm_ids`: up to 50 teigeodata IDs, comma-separated |

Point a Nominatim client, a geocoder plugin or a script at teigeodata and it works offline:

```sh title="tour.sh"
curl -s "$URL/search?q=Pokhara&format=jsonv2&limit=1"
```

```json title="Response"
[{"boundingbox":["28.26689","28.26689","83.968","83.968"],"display_name":"Pokhara, Pokhara, Kaski, Gandaki, Nepal","lat":"28.26689","licence":"Made with Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com), public domain; GeoNames (https://www.geonames.org), CC BY 4.0; Time zones: IANA Time Zone Database 2026f (public domain); Wikidata (https://www.wikidata.org), CC0 1.0; Unicode CLDR (https://cldr.unicode.org), Copyright © 1991-2026 Unicode, Inc., under the Unicode License v3; Local Government Directory, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Government of India (https://lgdirectory.gov.in); Administrative boundaries: Survey Department of Nepal and UN Resident Coordinator's Office in Nepal, via OCHA HDX (cod-ab-npl), CC BY-IGO 3.0; Elevation: NASADEM, NASA JPL and LP DAAC; Buildings: Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (https://cdla.dev/permissive-2-0/); Buildings: Google Open Buildings v3 (Sirko et al. 2021, arXiv:2107.12283), CC BY 4.0; Central Bureau of Statistics (now National Statistics Office), Nepal, via Open Data Nepal (https://opendatanepal.com), Creative Commons Attribution","lon":"83.968","name":"Pokhara","place_id":"tgd:np/1xhb"}]
```

A conformance corpus of real client requests is checked in CI. Differences from Nominatim, where
what cannot be filled is left out rather than faked:

- `place_id` is a teigeodata ID (a string); there is no `osm_type`, `osm_id`, `class`, `type` or
  `place_rank`, so `json` and `jsonv2` answer the same objects.
- `boundingbox` is the place's point (south = north, west = east), not its extent; draw an
  outline with the native `/boundary`.
- The address names the admin units by level as the country defines them.

## Errors [#errors]

A failure answers a stable code and an HTTP status:

```sh title="tour.sh"
curl -s -w '%{http_code}\n' "$URL/v1/reverse?lat=91&lon=0"
```

```json title="Response"
{"error":{"code":"invalid_argument","message":"91,0: the latitude is outside -90 to 90 degrees"}}
400
```

The codes and their statuses are listed in the [reference](/docs/reference/http#errors): `invalid_argument` and `out_of_bounds` answer 400 (a query string past the server's bound 414), `not_found` 404, `missing_component` 501, `unavailable` 503 and `internal` 500; `unauthenticated` 401, `forbidden` 403 and `rate_limited` 429 only from a deployment that adds keys, rules or limits.

## Deploying it [#deploying-it]

- **Bind it where you mean to.** It listens on loopback by default; behind a reverse proxy
  (Caddy, nginx), keep it there. With `--listen 0.0.0.0:8080` it answers anyone who can reach
  the port.
- **Limits are built in.** Every request is bounded (text length, `limit` at most 50, radius,
  time), so no request can make the server do unbounded work.
- **Floods and slow clients are bounded too.** Connections and requests in flight are capped.
  A request head must arrive within 10 seconds, and an idle HTTP/1 connection is closed after the
  same time. HTTP/2 peers are pinged every 20 seconds (and dropped when they stop answering) and
  get at most 32 streams each. A request past the in-flight
  cap is refused at once, never queued, so a client should retry after `Retry-After`. A reverse
  proxy in front still does TLS and per-client rate limits.
- **Updates without restarts.** Over a store, the server reads its journal every `--follow`
  seconds and serves newly installed or updated packs; queries in flight finish on the packs
  they started with.
- **Attribution** comes with every answer, from the packs that answered it; keep it visible
  where the data is shown.
- **MCP** is served at `/mcp` on the same port (Streamable HTTP): see [MCP server](/docs/servers/mcp).

# MCP server (/docs/servers/mcp)

The [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) lets an AI agent call tools. `tgd mcp`
gives it every teigeodata query as a tool: an agent can geocode a place, find what is at a
point, read a timezone or a height, and get the right answer from local packs instead of
guessing, with no API key and no network.

## Connect a client [#connect-a-client]

The client starts the server itself over standard input and output:

<Tabs items={["Claude Code","Claude Desktop","Any client"]}>
<Tab value="Claude Code">
```sh
claude mcp add teigeodata -- tgd mcp --pack /path/to/world-np-lite.tgd
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Claude Desktop">
```json title="claude_desktop_config.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "teigeodata": {
      "command": "tgd",
      "args": ["mcp", "--pack", "/path/to/world-np-lite.tgd"]
    }
  }
}
```
</Tab>

<Tab value="Any client">
Command `tgd`, arguments `mcp --pack <file>` (repeat `--pack` for several packs, or leave it out
to serve the store's installed packs). Over HTTP, `tgd serve` also answers MCP at `/mcp`
(Streamable HTTP) on its port.
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The server speaks MCP 2026-07-28 and 2025-11-25, and older clients too.

## Tools [#tools]

Every tool but `install` is read-only (`readOnlyHint`), declares its output schema, and returns the same
JSON as structured content and as text, with the attribution of the packs that answered.

| Tool | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `search` | Places matching a name, best first; "Name, Parent" and a focus point as in the API. |
| `reverse` | The places nearest a point, with distance and bearing. |
| `nearby` | The places nearest a place. |
| `get_place` | One place by its ID, optionally with every name it has. |
| `lookup` | Places by ID, in the order asked. |
| `admin_at` | The admin units holding a point, country first. |
| `hierarchy` | A place's ancestors up to its country. |
| `children` | A place's children, such as a country's provinces. |
| `timezone` | The IANA zone of a place or at a point, with its offset and abbreviation. |
| `elevation` | The terrain height at a point. |
| `postal` | Postal codes to places, by prefix, or at a point. |
| `boundary` | A unit's outline: a summary, and the GeoJSON as a resource. |
| `distance` | The distance and bearing between two points or places. |
| `packs` | The packs served, with their components and attribution. |
| `coverage` | The catalog's packs that cover a point (a server over a store). |
| `install`, `install_status` | Install catalog packs into the store, after the person confirms the size (a server over a store that allows it). |

Every argument, bound and answer field is in the [MCP tools reference](/docs/reference/mcp).

Long answers are paged with signed cursors, so an agent can never be handed more than its context
can hold. Packs and places are also **resources**: `teigeodata://dataset/…`,
`teigeodata://place/…` and `teigeodata://boundary/…`.

## Installs [#installs]

Over a store, `tgd mcp` lists `install` and `install_status`, so an agent that finds a place
outside the installed packs can offer to download its country. The person confirms the size
through the client (elicitation) before a byte is fetched; with a client that cannot ask, the
call installs only up to its own `max_bytes` (100 MB when left out), and a larger download answers
with the size and asks the agent to call again with `max_bytes` raised to it. `tgd mcp --no-install` leaves the tools out; `tgd serve` lists
them only with `--allow-install`.

## Try it [#try-it]

Ask your agent things like:

- "What's the timezone and the elevation of Namche Bazaar?"
- "Which district and province is 28.2096, 83.9856 in?"
- "List the provinces of Nepal with their ISO codes."
- "How far is Pokhara from Kathmandu as the crow flies?"

The agent calls `search`, `timezone`, `elevation`, `admin_at`, `children` and `distance`, and
answers from the packs, citing their sources.

# A GPS fix to a place (/docs/tutorials/gps-to-place)

A phone reports a latitude and longitude; the user wants to read where they are. Two queries
answer it: **reverse** gives what is *near* the point, and **admin units at a point** gives what
*holds* it. Together they make a label such as "331 m SE of Narayanhiti Royal Palace · Kathmandu, Bagmati".

<Steps>
<Step>
### Find the nearest places [#find-the-nearest-places]

`reverse` gives the places nearest the point, nearest first, each with `meters` and `bearing`
(degrees clockwise from north, from the place to the point).

<TourCode region="reverse" />

The first row is the "near" part of the label. To say "north-east of", turn the bearing into
one of eight directions: `["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"][round(bearing / 45) % 8]`.
</Step>

<Step>
### Find the units that hold the point [#find-the-units-that-hold-the-point]

`admin_at` tests the point against the admin boundaries and answers every unit it is inside,
country first. Near a border, the answer is the side the point is on, not the nearest centre.

<TourCode region="admin" />
</Step>

<Step>
### Put the label together [#put-the-label-together]

Take the nearest place with its distance and direction, then the units from the lowest level
up, leaving out the ones a reader does not need (most apps drop the ward, and the country at
home). For the point in step 1 (bearing 116°, so south-east):

```text
331 m SE of Narayanhiti Royal Palace · Kathmandu, Bagmati
```

The units are the same for every point in them, so an app tracking a moving user can keep the
last answer until the point leaves the lowest unit.
</Step>

<Step>
### Everything within a radius [#everything-within-a-radius]

For "what is around me" lists, `within_radius` gives every place within a distance, nearest
first, with the same columns:

<TourCode region="radius" />
</Step>
</Steps>

## Next [#next]

- [Reverse geocoding](/docs/guides/reverse) and [admin units](/docs/guides/admin) in full.
- [Outlines on a map](/docs/tutorials/map-outlines): draw the unit the user is in.

# In the browser (/docs/tutorials/in-the-browser)

`teigeodata-wasm` is the engine compiled to WebAssembly: the same calls as the
Node.js package, at most 256 KiB gzipped, or 150 KiB without name search. A page has no file
system, so it opens a pack from its bytes; after that one download, every query runs locally.
The [playground](/playground) is this package in a page.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Install [#install]

Install the package as the [install page](/docs/getting-started/install) shows (the
**Browser** tab). Bundlers (Vite, webpack, esbuild) treat the `.wasm` file as an asset, and the
package's `exports` pick the right entry for browsers, Node.js, Deno and Cloudflare Workers.
</Step>

<Step>
### Load the module and a pack [#load-the-module-and-a-pack]

`init()` loads and compiles the module once; then open the pack's bytes:

```js
import { init, Engine, Reader } from "teigeodata-wasm";

await init();
const engine = new Engine();
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch("/packs/world-np-lite.tgd")).arrayBuffer());
engine.openBytes(bytes);
```
</Step>

<Step>
### Keep the pack for offline visits [#keep-the-pack-for-offline-visits]

Serve the pack with a long `Cache-Control` and a content hash in its name, or keep it in the
Cache API or the origin private file system (OPFS), so a later visit opens it with no network.
</Step>

<Step>
### Query, off the main thread for large packs [#query-off-the-main-thread-for-large-packs]

Every query of the other languages works here:

<TourCode region="reverse" />

Opening copies the bytes into the module's memory once; queries then take microseconds. For a
pack of tens of megabytes, open it in a Web Worker so the page stays responsive while it loads.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Next [#next]

- [Install](/docs/getting-started/install), the **Browser** tab: `npm install teigeodata-wasm`,
  or a build from a checkout.
- [Measured](/docs/data/measured#webassembly-packages): the module sizes and their budgets.

# Overview (/docs/tutorials)

Each walkthrough takes one thing an app needs and builds it step by step, with every snippet
in every language. The code is cut from programs that ran on the released pack, so what you
copy works.

<Cards>
<Card title="A place search box" href="/docs/tutorials/search-box" description="Autocomplete that finds काठमाडौं, Kathmandu and Kathamandu, near the user first." />

<Card title="A GPS fix to a place" href="/docs/tutorials/gps-to-place" description="“331 m SE of Narayanhiti Royal Palace · Kathmandu, Bagmati” from a latitude and longitude." />

<Card title="Local time anywhere" href="/docs/tutorials/local-time" description="The zone, the offset and daylight saving at any point, without the device's clock rules." />

<Card title="Outlines on a map" href="/docs/tutorials/map-outlines" description="The district a user is in, drawn on MapLibre or Leaflet." />

<Card title="In the browser" href="/docs/tutorials/in-the-browser" description="The WebAssembly engine in a page or a worker, offline after one download." />

<Card title="Replace a Nominatim server" href="/docs/tutorials/replace-nominatim" description="Nominatim-compatible search and reverse from one pack and a few megabytes of memory." />
</Cards>

# Local time anywhere (/docs/tutorials/local-time)

A calendar, a prayer-time or sunrise app, a booking form: each needs the local time *at a
place*, not on the device. teigeodata answers it from the pack alone: the zone boundaries say
which zone a point is in, and the tzdb rules carried in the pack say its offset at any instant,
so an old phone with stale rules still gets it right.

<Steps>
<Step>
### The zone at a point [#the-zone-at-a-point]

`tz_at` gives the IANA zone the point falls in, as the zone boundaries draw it. Every place
also carries its zone in its `tz` column, so a place picked from search needs no second query.
</Step>

<Step>
### The offset at an instant [#the-offset-at-an-instant]

With the zone, `tz_offset_at` gives the UTC offset at a Unix time: seconds east of UTC, the
abbreviation, and whether daylight saving is in force. Nepal is `+0545` all year; New York
changes twice a year.
</Step>

<Step>
### Check that a local time exists [#check-that-a-local-time-exists]

When a user picks a wall-clock time, `tz_local` says whether it happens once (`unique`), never
(`gap`: the clocks skipped it) or twice (`overlap`: the clocks went back), with the offsets
before and after. A booking form should refuse the gap and ask which of the two in an overlap.

The three steps, in each language:

<TourCode region="timezone" />
</Step>

<Step>
### Know how fresh the rules are [#know-how-fresh-the-rules-are]

`tz_version` names the tzdb release the rules come from (`2026f` above). Governments change
their rules with short notice; a newer data release carries the new rules, and the
[store](/docs/concepts/store) updates installed packs.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Next [#next]

- [Timezones](/docs/guides/timezones) in full.
- [Elevation](/docs/guides/elevation): with the height of the point, sunrise and sunset times
  can account for the horizon dip.

# Outlines on a map (/docs/tutorials/map-outlines)

Show the user the district or municipality they are in, outlined on a map. The outline comes
from the pack as a GeoJSON Feature, the format every web map library reads.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Find the unit [#find-the-unit]

`admin_at` gives every unit that holds the point, country first. Pick the level you want to
draw: a district for an overview, the lowest level for a neighbourhood.

<TourCode region="admin" />
</Step>

<Step>
### Get its outline [#get-its-outline]

`boundary` answers the unit's outline as one row: `geojson` (an RFC 7946 Feature), the `lod`
read, its `tolerance_m` and the number of `vertices`. Level 0 is full resolution; 1 to 6 are
coarser, and neighbouring units still share their borders at every level.

<TourCode region="boundary" />

A country at level 0 can be megabytes: draw a coarser level, and keep 0 for measuring.
</Step>

<Step>
### Draw it [#draw-it]

The Feature goes to the map as it is. In MapLibre GL JS:

```js
map.addSource("unit", { type: "geojson", data: JSON.parse(row.geojson) });
map.addLayer({ id: "unit-fill", type: "fill", source: "unit", paint: { "fill-color": "#0b6e6e", "fill-opacity": 0.12 } });
map.addLayer({ id: "unit-line", type: "line", source: "unit", paint: { "line-color": "#0b6e6e", "line-width": 2 } });
```

Leaflet's `L.geoJSON(feature)`, OpenLayers' `GeoJSON` format, Shapely's `shape()`, Turf and
JTS read it too. The [playground](/playground) draws outlines this way.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Next [#next]

- [Outlines](/docs/guides/boundaries) in full, with every level of detail.
- [Accuracy](/docs/concepts/accuracy#boundaries-and-perspective): where the boundaries come
  from, and the perspective on disputed ones.

# Replace a Nominatim server (/docs/tutorials/replace-nominatim)

Clients written for Nominatim (geocoder plugins, mobile SDKs, scripts) call `/search`,
`/reverse` and `/lookup`. `tgd serve` answers those routes from a pack, alongside its own JSON
and GeoJSON API, with no database to import and no rate limit but your own.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Install the command line [#install-the-command-line]

```sh
cargo install --locked teigeodata-cli
```
</Step>

<Step>
### Get a pack and serve it [#get-a-pack-and-serve-it]

```sh
curl -LO https://github.com/teispace/teigeodata/releases/download/data-2026.11.14.3/world-np-lite.tgd
tgd serve world-np-lite.tgd
```

The server binds to loopback by default; put it behind your reverse proxy to expose it.
</Step>

<Step>
### Point the client at it [#point-the-client-at-it]

Clients set Nominatim's base URL to the server's. A search, as a client sends it:

```sh title="tour.sh"
curl -s "$URL/search?q=Pokhara&format=jsonv2&limit=1"
```

```json title="Response"
[{"boundingbox":["28.26689","28.26689","83.968","83.968"],"display_name":"Pokhara, Pokhara, Kaski, Gandaki, Nepal","lat":"28.26689","licence":"Made with Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com), public domain; GeoNames (https://www.geonames.org), CC BY 4.0; Time zones: IANA Time Zone Database 2026f (public domain); Wikidata (https://www.wikidata.org), CC0 1.0; Unicode CLDR (https://cldr.unicode.org), Copyright © 1991-2026 Unicode, Inc., under the Unicode License v3; Local Government Directory, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Government of India (https://lgdirectory.gov.in); Administrative boundaries: Survey Department of Nepal and UN Resident Coordinator's Office in Nepal, via OCHA HDX (cod-ab-npl), CC BY-IGO 3.0; Elevation: NASADEM, NASA JPL and LP DAAC; Buildings: Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (https://cdla.dev/permissive-2-0/); Buildings: Google Open Buildings v3 (Sirko et al. 2021, arXiv:2107.12283), CC BY 4.0; Central Bureau of Statistics (now National Statistics Office), Nepal, via Open Data Nepal (https://opendatanepal.com), Creative Commons Attribution","lon":"83.968","name":"Pokhara","place_id":"tgd:np/1xhb"}]
```
</Step>

<Step>
### Check what it holds [#check-what-it-holds]

`/search` takes `q` or the structured fields, `limit` (at most 40, as Nominatim),
`countrycodes`, `viewbox` and `bounded`; `/reverse` takes `lat`, `lon` and `zoom`. The
[HTTP server page](/docs/servers/http#nominatim-compatible) lists every parameter and
what differs from Nominatim.
</Step>
</Steps>

Measured on loopback, a pack answers tens of thousands of Nominatim searches a second with a
peak footprint of about 16 MB ([server load](/docs/data/measured#server-load)).

# A place search box (/docs/tutorials/search-box)

A user types into a box; under it, the right places appear as they type. This walkthrough
builds that box's engine side: one engine for the app, a query per keystroke, near places
first, and each row labelled with the units that hold it.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Open the pack once [#open-the-pack-once]

Open the engine when the app starts and keep it: opening maps the file and checks its head,
and each section is verified the first time a query reads it. One engine answers every
thread, so the search box and the rest of the app share it.

<TourCode region="open" />
</Step>

<Step>
### Search on each keystroke [#search-on-each-keystroke]

Pass what the user has typed so far. Search matches every name of every place, in every
script, and forgives typos, missing accents and abbreviations, so the box needs no
normalisation of its own. Ask for the few rows the box shows.

<TourCode region="search" />

On a low-end phone a keystroke is estimated at 1.3 ms at the 99th percentile
([measured](/docs/data/measured#phone-class-estimates)): fast enough to run on every keystroke
without a debounce, though off the UI thread is still the right place for it.
</Step>

<Step>
### Rank the places near the user first [#rank-the-places-near-the-user-first]

Many places share a name. Pass the user's location (or the middle of the map they are looking
at) as the **focus**: places near it rank first, the gain halving with every `focus_scale_m`
of distance.

<TourCode region="search-focus" />

For an autocomplete where an exact name must always be on top, set `strict`: rows rank by how
well the name matched (exact, loose, prefix, one edit, substring, two edits, phonetic), then
by importance and focus.
</Step>

<Step>
### Let users type the parent [#let-users-type-the-parent]

People write "Kathmandu, Bagmati" to mean the one in Bagmati. Search reads the part after the
comma as an ancestor of any level and ranks places inside it first; the box passes the text as
it is.

<TourCode region="search-parent" />
</Step>

<Step>
### Label each row [#label-each-row]

Two rows called "Pokhara" need their district and province to tell them apart. The ancestors
of a place give the label, parent first:

<TourCode region="hierarchy" />

Show the name and the first one or two ancestors ("Pokhara · Kaski, Gandaki"). When the user
picks a row, store its `id`: IDs survive data updates, and a merged place's old ID answers
with the survivor.
</Step>
</Steps>

- [Search](/docs/guides/search) in full: every option and column.
- [A GPS fix to a place](/docs/tutorials/gps-to-place): the reverse of this box.
